info.name: 21 · Admin user management
info.description:
The **admin account-management actions** on the user console: activate/deactivate an account, send someone a password-reset link, force-logout their sessions, and resend or revoke a pending invitation — each as a single-user route **and** through the platform bulk envelope.

**Flow.** A) invite a throwaway account, so there is a `pending` invitation to work with; B) **invitation** resend + revoke; C) **force-logout**, including proof that the target's existing token dies; D) **status** change; E) **password reset**; F) RBAC — what a non-admin cannot do.

**Permissions.** `users:update` gates status + password-reset, `users:invite` gates invitation resend/revoke, and `users:manage_sessions` gates force-logout. All three are **admin-only** except `users:invite`, which `owner` also holds.

**Contract notes — the account-status preconditions are the surprising part.**
- An **`invited`** account (invitation issued, never accepted) refuses a status change with **409** — *"only an active or inactive account can be activated or deactivated"* — and refuses a password reset with **409** — *"only an active account can be sent a password reset"*. So the status toggle is demonstrated on a seeded **active** user and restored afterwards.
- **force-logout works on any account**, `invited` included (204), and does invalidate the target's issued tokens — folder C proves that with a token captured before the call.
- **Deactivating an account also revokes its sessions**, not just future logins.
- ⚠ **Session revocation is second-granular and inclusive.** The marker is a Unix-second epoch and a token is rejected when `iat <= marker`, so a token minted *in the same second* as a revocation is already dead. **Folder C runs before folders D/E for exactly this reason** — its "the token worked before the call" baseline must not depend on a login that raced a revocation. If you reorder these folders, that assertion becomes flaky.
- `POST /auth/users/{id}/invitation/resend` **after** a revoke succeeds (**200**) and issues a fresh invitation — revoking does not blacklist the address.
- `POST /auth/invitations/bulk` row data requires **`role_ids`**, not just `email` — and it must be non-empty (an empty list is a `BadRequestError`). On this **platform** path `role_ids` *are* the account's global roles; there is no default fallback. Do not confuse it with the group-invitation path (`/evaluation-groups/{id}/invitations/bulk`), where the listed roles are group-scoped and a brand-new account separately gets the default `red_teamer` global role.
- All three bulk paths are the platform `BulkRequest` envelope: per-row savepoints, partial success, and `dry_run: true` reports without committing. An unknown `user_id` is a per-row **404**.

**⚠ This collection mutates seeded accounts.** Folder D deactivates and reactivates `viewer@test.com`, and folder C force-logs-out the viewer and the throwaway account. Everything is restored by the end, but do not run it concurrently with another collection that logs in as `viewer`.

**Auth model.** Per-request: `{{admin_token}}` acts, `{{owner_token}}` supplies the RBAC negatives. Self-contained — the throwaway account is deleted in teardown. No manual token (the emailed reset/invite tokens are never needed; only that the send is accepted).

**Prereq.** `make seedlocal`.

Folder **G** covers the role-management CRUD: `POST /roles` and `GET|PATCH|DELETE /roles/{role_id}`, with the guardrails that distinguish their near-identical refusals — a reserved slug vs a duplicate name (two different 409s), an unknown vs a non-delegable permission (two different 400s), and a system role refusing both a content edit (400, `is code-managed`) and a delete (400, not the default-role 409).

Verified green on a live stack: 94/94 assertions (Newman).

request.description: Holds `users:update`, `users:invite` and `users:manage_sessions` — every action here.
Holds `users:invite` but **not** `users:update` or `users:manage_sessions` — folder F's negatives.

item.name: 3 · Log in as viewer (token captured for folder C's force-logout baseline)

request.description: A seeded **active** account. Folder D toggles its status (and restores it); the token captured here is what folder C proves force-logout invalidates.
Holds none of `users:*` — supplies the `users:invite` denial in folder F, the one management permission `owner` *does* hold.
`roles:read` (admin). An invitation must name the roles to pre-assign, so the id is resolved from the API rather than hard-coded — role ids are generated per environment.

exec: pm.test('the seeded viewer is found', () => pm.expect(u).to.be.an('object'));

request.description: `users:read`. The status is asserted here so folder D starts from a known state — if a previous interrupted run left it `inactive`, this fails loudly instead of confusing the toggle.

**This is the only invite path** — the single-invite route is gone, so inviting one person is a one-row request. `role_ids` is **required** on the row data.

Duplicate emails in one envelope, or more than `MAX_INVITE_ROWS` (**100**) rows, are rejected as **422** at the envelope level — the ceiling is a schema `max_length` on `rows`, so it never reaches the service.

item.name: 2 · The account exists as `invited` with a pending invitation

exec: pm.test('status is invited, not active', () => pm.expect(u.status).to.eql('invited'));
pm.test('the invitation rides along on the projection', () => pm.expect(u.invitation.status).to.eql('pending'));

request.description: **FE note:** the user list embeds `invitation` (`status` + `expires_at`), which is what lets the console show "invited — expires in N days" and decide whether to offer *resend* or *revoke*. An `invited` account has no usable password yet.

exec: pm.test('still pending, for the same address', () => { pm.expect(b.status).to.eql('pending'); pm.expect(b.email).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('ua_email')); });
pm.test('the expiry was pushed out, not merely still valid', () => pm.expect(Date.parse(b.expires_at)).to.be.above(Date.parse(pm.collectionVariables.get('ua_expiry_before'))));

request.description: `users:invite`. Re-issues the single-use token and pushes the expiry out. Asserted against the expiry captured in folder A (`ua_expiry_before`) rather than against a bare 'still in the future' — the original invitation was in the future too, so that weaker form would hold even if resend refreshed nothing. The mail goes through the worker, so the token only ever appears in the worker log; this collection never needs it. (The margin is just the elapsed time between the two calls — `expires_at` is `now + TTL` — so it is tens of milliseconds, not days.)
`users:invite`. Marks the pending invitation `revoked` so the emailed link stops working.

exec: pm.test('no longer pending', () => pm.expect(u.invitation === null || u.invitation.status !== 'pending').to.eql(true));
pm.test('the account itself is untouched', () => pm.expect(u.status).to.eql('invited'));

request.description: Revoking the invitation does **not** delete the account — it stays `invited` with no live way in, which is the state an admin then either resends to or deletes.

exec: pm.test('a fresh pending invitation is issued', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql('pending'));

request.description: **Not** a 409. Revoking withdraws the outstanding link; it does not blacklist the address, so an admin who revoked by mistake can simply resend.
A well-formed id matching no live account.

item.name: 1 · The viewer's token works before the call

request.description: Establishes the baseline, so step 3 is a real before/after rather than an assumption.
`users:manage_sessions` — **admin-only**, separate from `users:update`, because revoking sessions is a containment action rather than an edit.

item.name: 3 · The same token is now rejected

request.description: **The assertion that matters.** An already-issued JWT stops being accepted, so force-logout is real session revocation and not merely a flag — that is the whole point when responding to a compromised account.

item.name: 4 · Force-logout works on an invited account too

request.description: Unlike status change and password reset, this has **no account-state precondition** — there is nothing to be inconsistent about in revoking sessions that may not exist.

exec: pm.test('the unknown user is a per-row 404', () => pm.expect(b.results.find(r => r.row_key === 'ghost').error.status).to.eql(404));

request.description: The "log everyone out" action, one row per account. Deliberately targets the throwaway account rather than a seeded one, so the rest of the suite keeps its sessions.
Force-logout revokes issued tokens; it does not disable the account, so a fresh login works immediately. Leaves the environment usable for the next collection.

item.name: 1 · An invited account cannot be deactivated → 409

exec: pm.test('explains which states are eligible', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('active or inactive'));

request.description:
The precondition worth knowing before wiring the console: `active` ⇄ `inactive` is the only legal toggle. An `invited` account has never been activated, so there is nothing to deactivate — **409**, not 422.

The console should therefore offer *resend/revoke* for an `invited` row and *activate/deactivate* only for an `active`/`inactive` one.

exec: pm.test('the full user projection comes back', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().email).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('viewer_email')));

request.description: `users:update`. The real toggle, on an account that is in an eligible state. ⚠ This mutates a seeded login — step 5 restores it.

item.name: 3 · A deactivated account cannot log in

exec: pm.test('and the reason is not disclosed', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.eql('Invalid email or password.'));

request.description:
What deactivation is *for*: correct credentials stop working.

**The error is deliberately generic.** A deactivated account, a wrong password and an address with no account all return the identical `401 Invalid email or password.` — so login cannot be used to enumerate which accounts exist or which are disabled. The distinction is recorded only in the structured log (`auth.login.failed` with `reason="inactive"` / `"unknown_email"`), never in the response, which is why this asserts the exact generic message rather than a reason code.

item.name: 4 · Bulk status: one eligible row, one ghost

exec: pm.test('the unknown user is a per-row 404', () => pm.expect(b.results.find(r => r.row_key === 'ghost').error.status).to.eql(404));
pm.test('the good row reports the new status', () => pm.expect(b.results.find(r => r.row_key === 'viewer').data.status).to.eql('active'));

request.description: The bulk path the console's multi-select uses. This call is also what **reactivates the viewer** — the good row commits despite its neighbour failing, which is the partial-success guarantee in action.

item.name: 5 · The viewer is active again and can log in

request.description: Confirms the seed state is restored, so the rest of the suite is unaffected. Re-captures the token for completeness; note that a token minted in the same second as the revocation just above is itself treated as revoked (see folder C), so nothing downstream relies on it.

exec: pm.test('reported as a dry run that would succeed', () => { pm.expect(b.dry_run).to.eql(true); pm.expect(b.succeeded).to.eql(1); });

request.description: A preview of a deactivation that must not happen — step 7 proves it did not.

item.name: 7 · …and the viewer really is still active

request.description: The assertion that gives step 6 its meaning.

item.name: 1 · An invited account cannot be sent a reset → 409

exec: pm.test('names the password-reset precondition, not the status one', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('can be sent a password reset'));

request.description: Stricter than the status toggle: a reset needs an **active** account (an `invited` one has no password to reset — it needs an *invitation*, not a reset). A distinct 409, so the console can offer the right action.

item.name: 2 · Send the seeded viewer a reset link

request.description:
`users:update`. **204** — the endpoint reports that the mail was *accepted*, not that it arrived: the send goes through the worker.

The single-use token is only ever written to the worker log (`email.sent.console`), never returned, so the reset link itself is out of reach for an automated run. Collection `01` documents the manual token dance for actually completing a reset.

exec: pm.test('reported as a dry run', () => pm.expect(b.dry_run).to.eql(true));
pm.test('the eligible row would succeed, the ghost would 404', () => { pm.expect(b.succeeded).to.eql(1); pm.expect(b.results.find(r => r.row_key === 'ghost').error.status).to.eql(404); });

request.description: Run as a **dry run deliberately** — a committed bulk reset would email every listed operator, which is not something a scenario collection should do to a shared environment. The per-row outcomes are still fully reported.
`users:update` is admin-only. The gate runs before body validation, so a well-formed body still gets the 403.
`users:manage_sessions` is admin-only too — an owner managing an engagement has no business ending other people's sessions.
The contrast that makes the split meaningful: `owner` holds `users:invite`, so onboarding is delegated while account control is not.

item.name: 4 · Owner cannot send a password reset → 403

request.description: Reset rides on `users:update`, not `users:invite` — being able to invite someone does not extend to resetting their credentials.

Completes the picture: `owner` holds `users:invite` (step 3 above) but `red_teamer` does not, so onboarding is delegated to owners only. Folder A/B exercised the allowed side of this permission; without this row the gate was only ever seen succeeding.
401 before 403: an anonymous caller is rejected for missing credentials, not for a missing permission.

item.name: G · Role CRUD

exec: pm.test('active but not any kind of default', () => { pm.expect(b.is_active).to.eql(true); pm.expect(b.is_default).to.eql(false); pm.expect(b.is_participant_default).to.eql(false); });

request.description: `roles:manage` (admin only). `name` is the slug and is immutable afterwards — `RoleUpdate` has no `name` field.
`roles:read`, which every role holds — unlike the write side.

exec: pm.test('names the reservation, not a plain collision', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('is reserved for a system role'));

request.description: A system slug is reserved even though no live *custom* role holds it — a different message from the duplicate case in step 4, which is the point of asserting the substring.

exec: pm.test('names the collision, not the reservation', () => { const d = pm.response.json().detail; pm.expect(d).to.include('already exists'); pm.expect(d).to.not.include('reserved'); });

request.description: Step 1's name, re-sent.

exec: pm.test('refused as an elevation vector, not as unknown', () => { const d = pm.response.json().detail; pm.expect(d).to.include('cannot be granted to a custom role'); pm.expect(d).to.include('roles:manage'); });

request.description: `NON_DELEGABLE_PERMISSIONS` — `roles:manage`, `users:manage_admin`, `users:update`. A custom role cannot hand out the keys to the role system itself.

exec: pm.test('a different refusal from the non-delegable one', () => { const d = pm.response.json().detail; pm.expect(d).to.include('Unknown permission'); pm.expect(d).to.not.include('cannot be granted'); });

request.description: A typo must not be silently dropped.

exec: pm.test('the slug did not — `RoleUpdate` carries no `name`', () => pm.expect(b.name).to.eql('custom-' + pm.collectionVariables.get('run_suffix')));

request.description: The slug is immutable by omission from the update schema, so this pins that a rename cannot move a role's identity.

exec: pm.test('says why, and that the flags are the exception', () => { const d = pm.response.json().detail; pm.expect(d).to.include('is code-managed'); pm.expect(d).to.include('activation and default flags'); });

request.description: `ua_role_id` is `red_teamer`, resolved in Setup step 5 — a system role. Only `is_active` / the default flags are editable on one; a display-name edit is refused.

exec: pm.test('a 400, not the 409 the default-role guard raises', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().detail).to.include('System role'));

request.description: System roles are code-managed: `make syncroles` would recreate one anyway. Distinct from the *default*-role guard, which is a 409.
Self-containment: the collection created it, so it removes it. Deletable because it is neither a system role, nor a default, nor the sole holder of anything.
Soft-deleted rows read as absent.

item.description:
The four role-management operations `POST /roles` and `GET|PATCH|DELETE /roles/{role_id}`, plus the guardrails that make them safe: a reserved slug and a duplicate name are two *different* 409s, an unknown and a non-delegable permission are two *different* 400s, and a system role refuses both a content edit and a delete. Writes need `roles:manage` (admin only); the read needs `roles:read`, which every role holds.

Self-contained: the custom role is created in step 1 and deleted in step 10, so a repeat run needs no cleanup. `run_suffix` keeps the slug unique in case a run is interrupted between the two.

request.description: `users:delete`. Soft delete; its invitation goes with it.
Soft-deleted, so even an admin holding `users:read` reads it as missing.

item.name: 3 · The seeded viewer is left active

exec: pm.test('restored to active, as the suite expects', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql('active'));

request.description: The final guarantee that this collection borrowed a seeded account and gave it back — the next collection to log in as `viewer` is unaffected.
